36.title: Looking under the lamp
36.hook: he lost his key inside the house but searches the street, because the light is better there
36.howItsDone: Nasruddin stories are told aloud across Turkish, Persian and wider Muslim cultures, often as a joke followed by a quiet moment of recognition; some Sufi teachers use them as teaching tales.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diogenes threw away his cup after a child beat him at living simply: less to carry. That closed week five. Today, a new week begins.

This week's teacher isn't an emperor or a philosopher. He's a fool. Or someone who looks like one. His name is Nasruddin. In Turkey he's Nasreddin Hodja; in Iran and Central Asia, Mulla Nasruddin. People have told short, funny stories about him for a long time, in many lands: at weddings, in coffee shops, to children at bedtime. Nobody knows for sure whether he was one real man. The stories belong to the people who tell them. Here's one.
screen: `A NEW KIND OF TEACHER: A FOOL.` → `TOLD IN MANY LANDS.` → `THE STORIES BELONG TO THE TELLERS.`

segments.voice: It's night. A neighbor finds Nasruddin on his hands and knees in the street, under a lamp. What have you lost, Mulla? My key, he says. So the neighbor gets down and helps. They search a long time: every stone, every crack. Nothing. Finally the neighbor asks: where exactly did you lose it? Oh, says Nasruddin, inside the house. Then why on earth are we looking out here? Because there's more light here. It's a joke, and you're allowed to laugh. That's how these stories work: first you laugh at the fool, and a few seconds later it's easy to notice he might be you. Looking where it's easy to look, not where things are, is a very human habit. Scientists even have a name for it now: the streetlight effect, studying what's easy to measure instead of what matters. People do it with bigger things than keys. Looking for peace in the next purchase, when the restlessness is somewhere inside. Looking for the fix to a relationship in a new city, when the trouble came along in the suitcase. Some Sufi teachers have told this tale as a picture of the soul, searching the bright outside world for something lost within. But the tale itself doesn't explain. Nasruddin stories rarely do. They just leave you standing in the street with the fool, both of you holding a very good lamp, and both of you knowing, now, where the key really is.
screen: `ON HIS KNEES UNDER A LAMP.` · `I LOST IT INSIDE THE HOUSE.` · `THERE'S MORE LIGHT HERE.` · `THE FOOL IS YOU.` · then, large: `SEARCH WHERE YOU LOST IT.`

segments.voice: Think of something bigger than a key that you've been searching for lately: calm, confidence, a better night's sleep, a closer friendship. Ask honestly which lamp you've been looking under, and where you actually lost it. Don't solve it; just let the answer point toward the house.
Nasruddin. A folk trickster who searches the street for a key he lost inside, because the light is better out there.
Your line: search where you lost it. A good lamp can't find what isn't there. See you tomorrow.

37.title: Eat, my coat
37.hook: turned away in rags, welcomed in a fur coat, he spoons the soup into his sleeve
37.howItsDone: In Turkey the saying "eat, my coat, eat" is still used to call out treatment based on appearances; many traditions teach hospitality that welcomes every guest the same, such as the Sikh langar and the Muslim and Jewish duty to honor the guest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nasruddin searched the street for a key he lost inside the house, because the light was better: search where you lost it.
screen: `LOOKING UNDER THE LAMP — SEARCH WHERE YOU LOST IT.`

segments.voice: Walk into a nice restaurant in sweatpants. Now walk in dressed up. Watch how the host looks at you, where they seat you, how fast the water arrives. Most of us have been on both sides of that look, and most of us have given it too, without meaning to. Nasruddin, the wise fool, got that look once, at a banquet in his own town. His answer became a proverb in Turkish, said to this day whenever someone is treated by their clothes and not by who they are.
screen: `SWEATPANTS, OR DRESSED UP?` → `THE LOOK AT THE DOOR.` → `A BANQUET IN HIS OWN TOWN.`

segments.voice: The story usually goes like this. There's a feast, and Nasruddin is invited. He comes straight from work in his everyday clothes, worn and dusty. Nobody greets him or finds him a seat. The dishes go around and somehow skip him. So he slips home and puts on his finest clothes: a big, beautiful fur coat. He walks back in, and everything changes. The host rushes over: welcome, welcome! He's seated near the top of the table, the best soup set in front of him. And Nasruddin dips the sleeve of his fur coat into the bowl and says: eat, my coat, eat! The guests stare. Mulla, what are you doing? Well, he says, it was the coat you welcomed. It seems only fair the coat should eat. In Turkish, eat, my coat, eat is a saying people still use, a whole sermon in three words. The old traditions knew this problem well. In Nasruddin's own Muslim world, a well-known saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, teaches that God does not look at your appearance or your wealth, but at your heart and your deeds. And a letter in the New Testament, from James, describes almost the same scene: a rich man in fine clothes is shown to the best seat, and a poor man in shabby clothes is told to stand at the back. Different homes, same banquet: the coat gets the soup, and the person goes hungry. Nasruddin doesn't lecture anyone. He just feeds the coat, and lets the whole room see what they've been doing.

segments.voice: Honestly, and without beating yourself up, think back over the last few days: was there someone you treated a little better, or a little worse, because of how they looked, what they wore, what they drove? The cashier, the new coworker, the person asking for change. Picture that person without the coat: just a person, hungry for the same things you are.
Eat. Nasruddin's words to his fur coat: eat, my coat, eat, because the coat was welcomed, and the man was not.
Your line: feed the person. The coat never needed the soup; the person did. Day thirty-seven.

38.title: Riding backward
38.hook: he rides his donkey facing the tail, and every town tells a different reason why (Nasruddin tale)
38.howItsDone: Nasruddin stories are told aloud across Turkey, Iran, Central Asia, the Balkans and beyond, often by parents and teachers, and each telling may give its own ending; he is often pictured riding his donkey backward.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nasruddin fed his soup to his fur coat, because the coat got the welcome he didn't: feed the person.

A dusty road in Anatolia, a long time ago. Here comes a man on a donkey, sitting backward: face toward the tail, back toward where he's going, perfectly calm about it. People in the market stop and stare. A child laughs. Somebody calls out: Hoca, you're on your donkey the wrong way! And Nasruddin, the teacher nobody can decide is a fool or a sage, has an answer ready. The trouble is, every town that tells this story gives him a different answer.
screen: `A MAN ON A DONKEY.` → `FACING THE TAIL.` → `EVERY TOWN, A DIFFERENT REASON.`

segments.voice: Here's one answer the tellers give. Nasruddin is riding to the school with his students walking behind him. If I face forward, he says, my back is to you, and that's rude. If you walk in front of me, your backs are to me, and that's rude too. So I ride facing you, and we can all see each other. Problem solved. In another telling, he just wants to see where he's been. In another, the donkey knows the way, so why watch the road? And in some, there's no reason at all: he rides backward, and the whole town argues about it. That's a clue to who Nasruddin is. The stories belong to Turkish, Persian and wider Muslim folk tradition, and they traveled far beyond it. Tradition places a real Nasreddin Hoca in thirteenth-century Anatolia, near the town of Akşehir, where a tomb bears his name. But many stories gathered around him over time, and nobody can say which, if any, he really lived. Hoca, in Turkish, means teacher: a teacher whose method is to do the ridiculous thing first and let you work out the lesson. The lesson here is about direction. We ride through our days facing forward, eyes on the next message, the next deadline. Nasruddin turns around. From the back of a donkey, the road already traveled is the whole view: who is walking with you, what you've passed. It isn't the wrong way. It's the other way, and it shows you what the front can't.
screen: `SO WE CAN SEE EACH OTHER.` · `ONE STORY, MANY ENDINGS.` · `HOCA MEANS TEACHER.` · `THE ROAD BEHIND IS THE VIEW.` · then, large: `NOT THE WRONG WAY. THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Start where you are and walk your day backward, one scene at a time, toward the moment you woke up, without judging any of it. Watch the road behind you the way Nasruddin does from his donkey: who was walking with you today, and one thing you passed without seeing. When you reach the morning, rest there.
Riding backward. Nasruddin on his donkey, facing the tail, so he can see the road behind him and the people walking with him. Today's word.
Your line: face the other way. The road behind you is part of the view. That's day thirty-eight.

39.title: You are right too
39.hook: as judge he tells both quarreling men they're right, and when his wife objects, tells her she's right too (Nasruddin tale)
39.howItsDone: Nasruddin's judge stories are told across Turkey, Iran and Central Asia, often to children and in classrooms, as a joke about snap judgments; in some tellings the objector is his wife, in others a clerk or a neighbor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nasruddin rode his donkey backward so he could see his students: face the other way.

Two friends, a couple, two coworkers, a family group chat. An argument breaks out, and both sides turn to whoever is watching: tell them I'm right. Be the judge. Somebody has to win. In the old stories, Nasruddin gets this job for real. For a while, the tales say, he serves as the town's judge, the qadi. Two men walk into his courtroom, red in the face, each sure the other has wronged him. Nasruddin settles into his seat and listens. What he says next is the whole joke.
screen: `TELL THEM I'M RIGHT.` → `NASRUDDIN, THE JUDGE.` → `TWO MEN, RED IN THE FACE.`

segments.voice: The first man tells his side. It's convincing. Nasruddin nods: you're right. The second man jumps in, furious, and tells his side. It's convincing too. Nasruddin nods: you're right. Then his wife, listening from the next room, and in some tellings it's a clerk or a neighbor, can't stand it. They can't both be right! Nasruddin thinks it over and says: you know, you're right too. It's a joke first. Let it be a joke. But look at what it catches. We tend to hear an argument as a contest with one winner, and we pick our winner fast, often before the second person has finished talking. Nasruddin can't. Each time someone speaks, he actually hears them, and finds something true. Quarrels are often like that: each side holds a real piece, a real hurt, a real fact, a real fear. The story cuts the other way too. A judge who agrees with everyone has decided nothing; the men still have their quarrel. Some things do need a decision, and the tale is laughing at Nasruddin as well. So it isn't telling you never to choose. It's asking you to notice how fast you choose, and what you miss when you do. Listen long enough to say, honestly, you're right, about something, to each person. Then decide, if you have to.
screen: `YOU'RE RIGHT. AND YOU'RE RIGHT.` · `WE PICK A WINNER FAST.` · `EACH SIDE HOLDS A REAL PIECE.` · `A JUDGE WHO DECIDES NOTHING.` · then, large: `YOU'RE RIGHT TOO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're close to, yours or someone else's, and let each person speak in your head. Find one thing each of them is right about; if you're one of the two, find what the other person is right about. Don't decide who wins: hold both, the way Nasruddin does, and breathe.
qadi, the Arabic word for judge. Nasruddin held that role, finding something true in each person who speaks, even the one who says they can't both be right.
Your line: you are also right. The joke is on the judge, too. Day thirty-nine, done.

40.title: The pot that died
40.hook: a borrowed pot "gives birth," later "dies," and the neighbor who believed the first can't refuse the second (Nasruddin tale)
40.howItsDone: Nasruddin's pot story is told across Turkey, Iran and Central Asia, and in Turkish the phrase "the cauldron gave birth" is still used, half joking, for a claim too good to be true.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nasruddin the qadi told both men they were right, then told the objector she was right too: you are also right.

You lend a neighbor your big cooking pot, the one for soup for twenty. A few days later there's a knock: your neighbor, holding your pot, and inside it, a tiny little pot. Congratulations, he says. While your pot was with me, it gave birth. This one's yours too. What do you do? You know pots don't give birth. But it's a free pot, and your neighbor is smiling. That neighbor is Nasruddin, and in Turkey this story lives on in a saying: the cauldron gave birth.
screen: `YOU LEND YOUR BIG POT.` → `IT GAVE BIRTH.` → `A FREE LITTLE POT.`

segments.voice: The neighbor takes the little pot. Of course he does. He doesn't argue with the miracle; he thanks Nasruddin and goes home happy. A few weeks later, Nasruddin knocks again. Could he borrow the big pot one more time? Gladly. Days pass. A week. No pot. Finally the neighbor goes over to ask for it back, and Nasruddin puts on a long, sad face. I'm so sorry. Your pot has died. Died? Don't be ridiculous. A pot can't die! And Nasruddin answers: you believed it could give birth. Why can't you believe it could die? The trap closes perfectly. The neighbor never believed the pot gave birth. He believed the free pot. The story was nonsense in his favor, so he let it pass, and the moment the same nonsense cost him something, he found his good sense again. Psychologists have a name for this: motivated reasoning. We check hard the claims we don't like, and wave through the claims we do: a compliment we'd love to be true, a shortcut that probably isn't allowed, a story about why the mess isn't our fault. Nasruddin's trick has a fairness to it. He never asks the neighbor to swallow a new kind of nonsense. He serves the same nonsense a second time, and holds the two halves side by side. The test he leaves is a simple one: before you accept a pleasant claim, ask, would I accept this if it cost me?
screen: `A POT CAN'T DIE!` · `HE BELIEVED THE FREE POT.` · `WE WAVE THROUGH WHAT WE LIKE.` · `WOULD I ACCEPT IT IF IT COST ME?` · then, large: `IF IT CAN GIVE BIRTH, IT CAN DIE.`

segments.voice: Think of something you believe that happens to suit you very well: that the rule doesn't really apply here, that you're too busy for that call, that someone else will handle it. Without arguing, ask it gently: would I believe you if you cost me something? Notice what happens in your chest, and just see the little pot for what it is.
kazan, Turkish for a big cooking pot. A neighbor who accepts one that gives birth can't refuse one that dies.
Your line: if it can give birth. If it can give birth, it can die. Forty days now.

41.title: The sermon he didn't give
41.hook: "do you know what I'll say?" and whatever the crowd answers, he finds a reason not to preach (Nasruddin tale)
41.carry: let those who know tell the others
41.howItsDone: The unpreached sermon is a Nasruddin tale told in Turkey, Iran, Central Asia and beyond, and its last line is sometimes borrowed by teachers who want a class to teach each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kazan that gave birth, and then died: if it can give birth, it can die.

A speaker clears his throat and says, I'll be brief. Forty minutes later, the back row is counting ceiling tiles. Nasruddin's sermon goes wrong the other way. The village has asked him to give the sermon, and the room fills up with people who've come to hear the famous teacher. He climbs up, looks out at all of them, and asks a single question: do you know what I'm going to say? Whatever they answer, he finds a way not to say it. Three weeks in a row.
screen: `I'LL BE BRIEF.` → `THE ROOM FILLS UP.` → `DO YOU KNOW WHAT I'LL SAY?`

segments.voice: The first week, the crowd answers honestly: no, we don't know. Then, says Nasruddin, I have nothing to say to people who don't even know what I'm talking about. He climbs down and goes home. The next week, they've worked it out. Do you know what I'm going to say? Yes! they shout. Then there's no need for me to tell you. Home again. The third week, they've made a plan: half the room shouts yes and half shouts no. Surely now he has to preach. Nasruddin smiles. Wonderful, he says. Let those who know tell those who don't. And he goes home. It's a trickster's escape, three times, and it's funny because he wriggles out of work every single week. But the last line is better than a joke. The crowd came to receive wisdom from one man at the front, and Nasruddin hands the job back to them. Half the room already knows something; the other half needs it. They don't need him standing between them. A lot of learning happens that way: not from the pulpit, but from the person in the next seat who figured it out last week. A grandmother showing how to fold the dough. A coworker who knows the shortcut. A friend who went through it first. Each of us is on the knowing side of something. So the question the story leaves isn't what Nasruddin would have said. It's what you know that someone near you doesn't, yet.

42.title: The smuggler
42.hook: for years a border guard searches his saddlebags and finds nothing, because he was smuggling donkeys (Nasruddin tale)
42.howItsDone: The smuggler is one of the Nasruddin tales most often retold in teaching and business talks as a picture of missing the obvious; in Iran and Central Asia he is usually called Mulla Nasruddin, in Turkey Nasreddin Hoca.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the khutba Nasruddin never gave: let those who know tell the others. Today, the last day of Nasruddin's week.
screen: `LET THOSE WHO KNOW TELL THE OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Ever hunted the whole house for your glasses while they sat on your head? Or searched for your phone using its own flashlight? The thing you're missing is often the thing you're holding. Today, a border guard with that problem, for years. Every week, a man comes across the frontier leading a donkey loaded with bundles of straw. And every week the guard is sure he's smuggling something. He can see it in the man's face, in his new clothes, in his growing house. The man is Nasruddin.
screen: `GLASSES ON YOUR HEAD.` → `A DONKEY, SOME STRAW.` → `THE GUARD IS SURE.`

segments.voice: The guard does everything right. He unties the bundles and shakes out every stalk. He checks the saddlebags, pats Nasruddin down, looks in his shoes, sometimes even burns the straw to see if something's hidden in it. Nothing. Week after week, nothing, and week after week, Nasruddin gets richer. Years pass. Both men grow old. The guard retires, and one day, in another town, he spots Nasruddin in a teahouse and sits down beside him. Please, he says, I'm not a guard anymore. You can tell me now. What were you smuggling? Nasruddin sips his tea: donkeys. That's the whole secret. The guard was so busy searching what the donkey carried that he never looked at the donkey, walking past him every week, in plain sight, the whole point. We do the same: search the details, miss the obvious. A worried parent checks every homework answer and misses that the child is sad. A company counts every expense and misses that its best people are leaving. You look for what's wrong in a friendship and miss that you haven't called in months. Now look back at the week. Nasruddin searched under the lamp because the light was better. He fed soup to his coat. He rode backward. He told everyone they were right. His pot gave birth and died. He never gave the sermon. And today, he walked the answer right past the guard. Seven stories, one teacher, and each time the lesson was in plain sight, disguised as a joke.

segments.voice: Think of a problem you've been searching hard, stalk by stalk through the straw. Now step back and look at the whole donkey: what walks right past you every week that you've stopped noticing, a tiredness, a person, a habit, a gift? Don't solve it; just name it quietly, once.
The smuggler. A guard searches the straw for years, and never sees that the thing crossing the border is the donkey. Today's word.
Your line: it's the donkey. The answer was never in the straw. That's Nasruddin's week.
